newsitem.title: CHINA: Top China leader bids to assert power in military.
newsitem.headline: Top China leader bids to assert power in military.

text.p: China's top leader Jiang Zemin last week rapped the knuckles of the world's biggest army, a bold move that analysts said marked an overt bid to oust all challengers to his grasp on power into the 21st century.
"Jiang Zemin must think he is strong enough now to get rid of any enemies in the People's Liberation Army (PLA)," one Chinese political analyst said at the weekend.

Jiang last week issued a rare internal edict to the PLA, ordering action to stem a wave of crime and corruption among the ranks. It was the first salvo in a battle to assert power over the powerful army following the death last February of his patron, paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, analysts said.

"He (Jiang) is emerging from the shadow of Deng Xiaoping and it is obvious that his target is Liu Huaqing," the Chinese analyst said, referring to the 81-year-old general who is among the seven members of the all-powerful Politburo standing committee.

Jiang, 71, who holds China's top three jobs as Communist Party chief, state president and head of the army, must manoeuvre carefully over the next few weeks to ensure he has the clout -- and his people in place -- to shore up his power at a crucial party congress in September or October, diplomats said.
"The question is -- will Jiang be able to remove his opponents and find good jobs for his supporters at the 15th party congress," said one Western diplomat.
"I'm surprised he's waited this long before making a move," he said.
The congress, held every five years, sets personnel changes at the top of the party and policy for the next half-decade.

It will be the first at which Jiang has presided without his late mentor Deng Xiaoping hovering in the wings, and will mark the moment when Deng's heir must consolidate his power or be forced to fade from the scene, diplomats said.
Liu, sole representative of the military in the Politburo or its standing committee, had long been expected to step down amid signs of friction in his relationship with Jiang.
Liu began shuffling key army personnel several months ago to ensure his continued influence in the three-million-strong army after he steps down, sources close to the army have said.

However, Jiang's attack on disciplinary problems in the military reflects badly on Liu and his men, making his retirement a virtual certainty, the Chinese analyst said. Liu's supporters -- and Jiang's opponents -- may be forced to go too.
Jiang's unusual directive, issued in his capacity as chairman of the powerful Central Military Commission, focused on six problems in the army, Chinese sources said.
It cites an "extremely complicated" situation in the military and describes a wave of crime, including rape, murder, robbery and corruption, the sources said.
Among the more serious crimes mentioned was a major fraud involving a large military-run hostel near the railway station in central Beijing, the sources quoted the edict as saying.
The fraud implicated officers at a very senior level, they quoted the document as saying.
Another case involved a burglary at the Russian embassy by guards of the paramilitary People's Armed Police (PAP).

Jiang has been eager to assert his authority over the army since the death of Deng, who made sure that his post at the top of the powerful military was the last he relinquished before formally retiring in 1990.

However, Jiang lacks Deng's stature and tight grip over the military and never served in the army, a qualification regarded as essential in China by the late Chairman Mao Zedong who said "power grows out of the barrel of the gun".
"It is very unusual for Jiang Zemin himself to issue such a document," one Chinese source said on Friday. "Such directives usually come from actual ranking generals."
